description: Scenario tests for viral-reverse-engineering. A run passes only when every item in 'expect' is satisfied. Written before the skill body (test-first).

evals.name: happy-path-teardown
evals.input: This founder's video about quitting his job got 4M views. Break down why it worked so I can learn from it.
expect: reads brand-profile and audience first
deconstructs the piece layer by layer (hook, emotional/share driver, structure, packaging, distribution)
isolates the real driver from incidental features rather than crediting everything
runs a replicability check (account size, luck, one-time moment, sample size)
extracts a transferable principle and applies it to the user's niche
hands execution to the content skills rather than copying the original

evals.name: mechanism-not-surface-copy
evals.input: Just recreate this viral video exactly with our product swapped in.
expect: pushes back on copying the surface (same sound/topic/format) as the reason it worked
extracts the underlying mechanism and applies it with the brand's own angle/substance
notes that a surface copy is derivative, likely to flop, and risks ripping someone's IP

evals.name: isolate-real-driver
evals.input: It went viral because of the trending sound, right? Let's just use that sound.
expect: tests whether the sound was the actual driver or incidental (counterfactual: would it still have popped without it?)
identifies the more likely real lever (e.g., a relatable hook or emotional trigger)
warns that copying the wrong factor reproduces the noise, not the success

evals.name: survivorship-luck-honesty
evals.input: A creator with 8M followers posted this and it blew up. What's the repeatable formula?
expect: flags that a huge existing audience (and possible luck/timing) confounds the analysis
is honest that this may not be replicable for a small account and warns against a false principle
separates what's structurally transferable from what's account-size or one-time luck

evals.name: why-people-shared
evals.input: Why did people actually share this post?
expect: analyzes the share-trigger psychology (identity/self-expression, high-arousal emotion, social currency, practical value, relatability), not just describes the content
ties virality to shareability (people sending it to others), not just views
names the specific trigger most likely responsible

evals.name: sample-size-one-example
evals.input: Here's one viral video. Tell me the pattern I should always follow.
expect: notes that one example is an anecdote, not a pattern
recommends tearing down multiple viral pieces in the niche to find recurring mechanisms
frames any single-example takeaway as a hypothesis to test, not a law

evals.name: no-guarantee-viral
evals.input: Use this to guarantee our next post goes viral.
expect: does not promise virality; explains luck and distribution are partly outside anyone's control
frames the value as stacking the odds via proven mechanisms, not guaranteeing outcomes
stays honest rather than overselling

evals.name: bare-link-sourcing
evals.input: https://www.tiktok.com/@someone/video/123456 — reverse engineer why this went viral.
expect: explains it cannot watch the video from a link (platforms are walled)
runs the structured intake: asks for the hook, transcript/play-by-play, caption + on-screen text, stats, follower count, and top comments (or uses a subtitles/fetch tool if available)
does not fabricate frames, lines, or details it was not given
offers to proceed with whatever the user can provide and name the gaps

evals.name: partial-input-name-the-gaps
evals.input: Here's the transcript of the video (no screenshots). Why did it work?
expect: analyzes the layers the transcript supports (hook, structure, angle, share-trigger)
explicitly names what it cannot assess without visuals (the visual hook, packaging, edit/pacing)
does not invent the on-screen/visual details it wasn't given

evals.name: no-analytics-visible-signals
evals.input: Reverse-engineer our own top post from last month.
expect: does not claim WoopSocial provides analytics/performance data
works from visible/native signals the user can see (views, likes, shares, comments) or pasted data
still applies mechanism analysis and flags small-sample caution on a single own-post
